rare

/RAIR/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Rare means not occurring often; uncommon; found in small numbers.

Rare means not occurring often or found only in small numbers — like a bird so rare that even lifelong birdwatchers may never spot one.

Example

Halley's Comet makes a rare appearance in Earth's skies, swinging close enough to see only once every 75 years or so.

An event that comes around once in 75 years is about as infrequent as sky-watching gets. Rare captures exactly how seldom something happens or how few of it exist.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

infrequent: Infrequent means not happening often, said of events and repetitions — infrequent visits, infrequent buses. It counts occurrences over time. Rare covers that and more: rare also describes things few of which exist at all, like a rare coin, which exists in tiny numbers rather than happening seldom.

atypical: Atypical means not matching the usual type or pattern — an atypical response, atypical weather for June. Something atypical breaks the mold, however often it occurs. Rare is purely about numbers and frequency: few exist, or it seldom happens. A rare event can be perfectly normal in kind, just seldom seen.

sporadic: Sporadic means occurring at irregular, unpredictable intervals — sporadic gunfire, sporadic protests. It describes scattered timing, not low frequency. Rare means it seldom happens or few exist, however regular the schedule. Halley's Comet is rare but not sporadic: its visits are precisely timed, seventy-five years apart.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

common: found everywhere; ordinary

frequent: happening often

Where it sits · how seldom it turns up

uncommon → rare → unheard-of

uncommon vs. rare: An uncommon sight turns a few heads but still shows up now and then; a rare one might appear only a handful of times in a lifetime.

unheard-of vs. rare: Unheard-of goes further still — something so rare that most people don't believe it happens at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rarus: thinly spread; loosely packed; infrequent (Latin)

Put it together: Rare comes straight from Latin rarus, "thinly spread" — picture items scattered so thinly across the world that you seldom come across one.

Use the root in a new word: rarefied: Climbers pause every few steps in the rarefied air near the summit, drawing long breaths that never feel like enough.

Word Building

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday — near-synonym alert

Rare and its unit-mate scarce overlap but are not identical: rare means few exist or it seldom happens (a rare coin, a rare visit), while scarce usually means something is temporarily hard to get relative to demand (water grew scarce during the drought). Rare also has an unrelated cooking sense — a rare steak is one cooked only lightly.
